'''Steven Peter Russell Rose''' (4 July 1938 – 9 July 2025) was an English neuroscientist, author and social commentator. He was a professor of biology and [[neurobiology]] at the [[Open University]] and [[Gresham College, London|Gresham College]], London.

==Early life==
Born in London, England on 4 July 1938,<ref>"ROSE, Prof. Steven Peter Russell", ''Who's Who 2013'', A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 2013; online edn, Oxford University Press, December 2012; online edn, November 2012. [http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U33166 Retrieved 6 August 2013]</ref> he was brought up as an [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodox Jew]]. Rose said that he decided to become an [[atheist]] when he was eight years old.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Steven P. |editor1-last=Holloway |editor1-first=Richard |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oAkj3sqKNG0C&pg=PA41 |chapter=In the Beginning |title=Revelations: Personal Responses to the Books of the Bible |page=[https://archive.org/details/revelationsperso0000unse_q0w9/page/41 41] |publisher=[[Canongate Books]] |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-84195-737-1 |quote=Did the editors of this series of volumes of the King James realise that I was an ex-Orthodox Jew, an atheist and a biologist to boot when they suggested that I write this introduction? |url=https://archive.org/details/revelationsperso0000unse_q0w9/page/41 }}</ref> He went to a direct grant school in northwest London which operated a ''[[numerus clausus]]'' restricting the numbers of Jewish students. He studied [[biochemistry]] at [[King's College, Cambridge]], and neurochemistry at the [[Institute of Psychiatry]], [[King's College London]].<ref name=mm>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/radio4/religion/steven_rose.shtml Biography at ''The Moral Maze''.]</ref>

==Academic career==

Following a Fellowship at [[New College, Oxford]], and a [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]] research post, he was appointed to the professorship of biology at the newly instituted Open University in 1969. At the time he was Britain's youngest full professor and chair of the department. At the Open University he established the Brain Research Group, within which he and his colleagues investigated the biological processes involved in [[memory formation]] and treatments for [[Alzheimer's disease]] on which he published some 300 research papers and reviews. He wrote several [[popular science]] books and regularly wrote for ''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper and the ''[[London Review of Books]]''. From 1999 to 2002, he gave public lectures as a professor of Physick (Genetics and Society) with his wife, the feminist sociologist [[Hilary Rose (sociologist)|Hilary Rose]] at [[Gresham College]], London. His work won him numerous medals and prizes including the [[Biochemical Society]] medal for communication in science and the prestigious [[Edinburgh Medal]] in 2004. His book ''The Making of Memory'' won the [[Rhone-Poulenc Science Book Prize]] in 1993.<ref name="Biography">{{cite web | url=http://www.stevenroseonline.net/SPRR/Long_bio_.html | title=Biography | publisher=Steven Rose Online | access-date=26 April 2018}}</ref>

Together with Hilary Rose he was a founder member of the [[British Society for Social Responsibility in Science]] in the 1960s, and more recently they have been instrumental in [[Academic boycotts of Israel#Guardian open letter.2C 2002|calling for a boycott of]] Israeli academic institutions for as long as Israel continues its [[Israeli-occupied territories|occupation of the Palestinian Territories]], on the grounds of Israeli academics' close relationship with the [[Israel Defense Forces|IDF]]. An open letter<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/Archive/Article/0,4273,4388633,00.html |title=Open Letter: More pressure for Mid East peace |work=The Guardian |date=6 April 2002}}</ref>  initiated by Steven and Hilary Rose, and also signed by 123 other academics was published in ''[[The Guardian]]'' on 6 April 2002.<ref>{{cite news |first1=Andy |last1=Beckett | author1-link = Andy Beckett |first2=Ewen |last2=MacAskill | author2-link =Ewen MacAskill |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk_news/story/0,3604,858363,00.html |title=British academic boycott of Israel gathers pace |work=The Guardian |date=12 December 2002}}</ref> In 2004 Hilary Rose and he were the founding members of the [[British Committee for the Universities of Palestine]].<ref name="Biography"/><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.bricup.org.uk/December09tour.html | title=BRICUP UK tour Dec 09 | publisher=BRICUP | date=2 December 2013 | access-date=26 April 2018 | archive-date=23 September 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923194517/http://www.bricup.org.uk/December09tour.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>

Rose was for several years a regular panellist on [[BBC Radio 4]]'s ethics debating series ''[[The Moral Maze]]''.<ref name=mm/> He was a Distinguished Supporter of [[Humanists UK]]. He was part of the [[Royal Society]]'s working group producing their Brain Waves modules on the state of neuroscience and its social framing, and was a member of the [[Nuffield Council on Bioethics]] Working Party on ''Novel Neurotechnologies''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nuffieldbioethics.org/neurotechnology/neurotechnology-about-working-party |title=Neurotechnology – About the Working Party &#124; Nuffield Council on Bioethics |access-date=26 May 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130613220325/http://www.nuffieldbioethics.org/neurotechnology/neurotechnology-about-working-party |archive-date=13 June 2013  }}{{full citation needed|date=September 2018}}</ref> His recent books with Hilary Rose include ''Alas Poor Darwin: Arguments against Evolutionary Psychology'', in 2012, ''Genes, Cells and Brains: the Promethean promises of the new biology'' (Verso), described by ''Guardian'' reviewer [[Steven Poole]] as "fascinating, lucid and angry" with a "lethally impressive hit ratio", and most recently ''Can Neuroscience Change Our Minds?'' (Polity, 2016). His audio-autobiography forms part of the [[British Library]]'s National Life Stories Collection of distinguished scientists. The sociologist [[Nikolas Rose]] is his younger brother. Hilary and he had two sons. He remained an atheist.<ref>"Lifeline: Steven Rose", ''[[The Lancet]]'' Vol. 355, Issue 9213, p. 1472, 22 April 2000.</ref>

Rose was a defender of the use of animals in medical research, accepting the description of himself as a "vivisector".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rose |first=Steven |date=2004-07-29 |title=Why I experiment on animals |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2004/jul/29/lastword.research |access-date=1 June 2026 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The issue of animal rights was debated by him and [[Jolyon Jenkins]] in the pages of ''[[New Statesman and Society]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 June 1991 |title=The rights or otherwise of animals are debated here between STEVEN ROSE and JOLYON JENKINS |url=https://www.greenleft.org.au/1991/18/rights-or-otherwise-animals-are-debated-here-between-steven-rose-and-jolyon-jenkins-both |access-date=1 June 2026 |website=Greenleft}}</ref>

In 2012 the [[British Neuroscience Association]] gave him a lifetime award for "Outstanding contributions to neuroscience."{{citation needed|date=December 2019}}

== Critique of genetic determinism ==

{{see also|Biological determinism}}

With [[Richard Lewontin]] and [[Leon Kamin]], Rose championed the "radical science movement".<ref>{{cite book |first1=Steven Peter Russell |last1=Rose |first2=Richard Charles |last2=Lewontin |first3=Leon J. |last3=Kamin |year=1984 |title=Not in Our Genes: Biology, Ideology and Human Nature |page=ix |publisher=Penguin Books |isbn=978-0-14-022605-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.madinamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/2018-Endnotes-for-Jay-Joseph-Mad-In-America-Blog-Leon-Kamin.pdf | title=Endnotes for "Leon J. Kamin (1927-2017): A Nemesis of Genetic Determinism and Scientific Racism" | work=[[Mad in America]] | date=4 April 2018 | access-date=26 April 2018 | author=Jay Joseph, PsyD}}</ref> The three criticized [[sociobiology]], [[evolutionary psychology]], and [[adaptationism]], most prominently in the book ''[[Not in Our Genes]]'' (1984), laying out their opposition to [[Sociobiology: The New Synthesis|''Sociobiology'']] ([[E. O. Wilson]], 1975), ''[[The Selfish Gene]]'' ([[Richard Dawkins]], 1976), and other works promoting an evolutionary explanation for human social behaviour. ''Not in Our Genes'' described Dawkins as "the most reductionist of sociobiologists". In retort, Dawkins wrote that the book practices a [[straw man]] fallacy by distorting arguments ''in terms'' of genetics to "an idiotic travesty (that the properties of a complex whole are simply the ''sum'' of those same properties in the parts)", and accused the authors of giving "ideology priority over truth".<ref name=socioreview>{{cite journal |first1=Patrick |last1=Bateson | author-link = Patrick Bateson |first2=Richard|last2=Dawkins |date=24 January 1985 |title=Sociobiology: the debate continues |journal=[[New Scientist]] |volume=105 |issue=1440 |pages=28–60 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D-SquR8DyUsC&pg=PA58}}</ref> Rose replied in the second edition of his book ''Lifelines''. Rose wrote further works in this area: in 2000 he jointly edited with the sociologist [[Hilary Rose (sociologist)|Hilary Rose]], a critique of evolutionary psychology entitled ''Alas, Poor Darwin: Arguments Against Evolutionary Psychology''. In 2006 he wrote a paper dismissing classical [[heritability]] estimates as useful scientific measures in respect of human populations especially in the context of [[IQ]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1093/ije/dyl064 |title=Commentary: Heritability estimates—long past their sell-by date |year=2006 |last1=Rose |first1=Steven Peter Russell |journal=[[International Journal of Epidemiology]] |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=525–7 |pmid=16645027|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Rose wrote the introduction of ''The Richness of Life'' (2007) by the prominent American paleontologist, evolutionary biologist, and historian of science, [[Stephen Jay Gould]].

[[J. Richard Udry]] dismissed Rose's ''Lifelines'' criticisms of genetic determinism, stating they were straw men.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Udry |first=J. Richard |date=1 October 1999 |title=How to alienate your natural allies and attract your enemies |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/how-to-alienate-your-natural-allies-and-attract-your-enemies/129FFF02164CD1B3C2C9FDF381A11586 |journal=[[Behavioral and Brain Sciences]] |volume=22 |issue=5 |pages=911–911 |doi=10.1017/S0140525X99502203 |access-date=11 May 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A. J. Wells asserted that Rose created a false dichotomy between homeodynamic and [[Neo-Darwinism|neo-Darwinian]] explanations for human behavioural patterns, and like Udry, said that Rose's portrayal of "ultra-Darwinism" was a caricature of the views of evolutionary behaviourists.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wells |first=A. J. |date=1 October 1999 |title=Rose's homeodynamic perspective is not an alternative to neo-Darwinism |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/roses-homeodynamic-perspective-is-not-an-alternative-to-neodarwinism/F09874A53015DA98C50D67D330E19AB0 |journal=[[Behavioral and Brain Sciences]] |volume=22 |issue=5 |pages=911–912 |doi=10.1017/S0140525X9951220X |access-date=11 May 2026 |via=Cambridge Core}}</ref> Nicholas S. Thompson lampooned Rose for suggesting behavioural geneticists were trying to rehabilitate [[Nazism]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Thompson |first=Nicholas S. |date=1 October 1999 |title=High purpose, low execution |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/high-purpose-low-execution/35547962B903ECE0E5E619C67E588C8D |journal=[[Behavioral and Brain Sciences]] |volume=22 |issue=5 |pages=910–911 |doi=10.1017/S0140525X99492209 |access-date=11 May 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Death ==
Rose died on 9 July 2025, at the age of 87.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ferry |first=Georgina |date=10 July 2025 |title=Steven Rose obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2025/jul/10/steven-rose-obituary |access-date=11 July 2025 |newspaper=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>
